title: AI agent or AI assistant: which does your team need?
description: Which workflows need an AI agent, which need an assistant, who approves each step, how agents are priced, and our check of nine agent products.
job: deciding whether a workflow needs an AI agent, an AI assistant or neither
verdict: Pick an AI assistant (generative AI) if the work is drafting, summarizing or answering, and a person acts on it[^2][^6].
Pick an AI agent if the work crosses several systems, needs judgment calls, and a named person approves risky steps[^6][^10].
Pick neither if the steps never change; plain rules automation is cheaper and more predictable[^8][^5].
Pick short, supervised agent tasks over long unattended ones; the best agent finished under a third of test office tasks[^14][^7].
Ask every vendor who approves and what it bills; only four of nine we checked gate risky steps by default[^33][^6].

onPage.text: Which workflows suit an assistant, an agent or neither

headings.what-goes-wrong: How do you spot agent washing and other mistakes?

summary: An AI assistant is generative AI: it drafts, summarizes or answers, and a person acts on it[^2][^3]. An AI agent is agentic AI: given a goal, it plans steps and acts in your systems[^1][^5]. What makes or breaks an agent is what it may touch and who approves risky steps[^10][^11].

recipes.name: 1. Start with an assistant (most teams, first 90 days)
recipes.when: An ops team of 10 to 30 whose work is drafting, summarizing and answering policy questions, with no system changes[^6][^17].
flow: Ops lead: picks three repeat tasks, such as the weekly report, vendor emails and procedure lookups
Staff member: asks the assistant for a draft
Staff member: checks and edits it, then sends or files it
Ops lead: once a month, compares time per task against the starting baseline
recipes.cost: Per seat: Microsoft 365 Copilot Business is $21 a user a month, so 15 people cost about $315[^21]. Claude Team Standard read $25 monthly or $20 annual in our 22-26 Nov check; we didn't capture ChatGPT Business's figure[^26][^25].

recipes.name: 2. One narrow agent with an approval step (service team)
recipes.when: High-volume, repeatable requests with clear rules, such as order status, password resets and simple returns[^8][^23].
flow: Head of service: writes the rules and lists the actions the agent may take
Admin: grants read access plus only those actions, and turns on confirmation for refunds, cancels and account changes[^24][^30]
Agent: answers the customer and runs the allowed lookups
Service rep: approves any refund or account closure the agent proposes[^30]
Head of service: reviews a sample of resolved conversations each week, and tracks resolution time against the starting baseline
recipes.cost: Vendor list prices, read 26 Nov 2026: Agentforce is $0.10 an action, about $120 a month in Salesforce's own order-status example[^23]. Intercom Fin is $0.99 per resolved outcome plus seats from $29; Zendesk charges $1.50 to $2.00 per automated resolution[^30][^29].

recipes.name: 3. A back-office agent with a role-owned gate (AP exceptions)
recipes.when: A finance or ops team with many exceptions a month across email, the ERP (finance system) and documents, each needing a judgment call[^6][^17].
flow: Controller: records today's exception count and handling time as the baseline
Controller: sets the decision rules and the approval threshold, such as any payment change or credit over a set amount
IT or admin: connects the agent to the inbox and ERP with the narrowest rights, and no payment release[^10][^11]
Agent: reads the invoice, matches the PO, finds the gap, drafts the vendor email and proposes a fix
AP specialist: approves, edits or rejects each proposal in an approval queue[^22][^31]
Controller: signs off anything over the threshold and reviews the log of agent actions monthly[^12]
recipes.cost: Microsoft Copilot Studio is $200 per 25,000 credits a month, or pay as you go; credits used per action vary[^21]. UiPath and ServiceNow price agents by consumption units or per action, with no dollar price published[^31][^28].

humanRole: Ops lead or system owner decides what the agent may touch. Give it the fewest functions, permissions and autonomy the task needs[^10][^11].

The role owner, such as the AP specialist, controller or service rep, approves high-impact or hard-to-reverse actions before they run[^10][^11]. ChatGPT Work and Claude in Chrome build this check in[^25][^26].
A team lead reviews a sample of agent work on a schedule. NIST's risk framework asks that human oversight be defined, assessed and documented[^12].
Leadership decides which decisions agents never make, and matches controls to each agent's level of autonomy[^9][^7]. Most real deployments today run under significant human oversight[^3].

Pages change often: ChatGPT agent became ChatGPT Work, Zendesk is changing its model and Google removed its price cards.

example.input: Illustrative, not a client case: a vendor emails an invoice that is $480 over its purchase order. With an assistant, the AP specialist pastes both in and gets the gap and a polite email draft[^2]. The specialist then checks the ERP, sends the email and logs the case.
example.output: With an agent, it reads the inbox, pulls the PO from the ERP, finds the $480 gap, drafts the email and proposes a hold[^1][^4]. The AP specialist approves or edits one card; the controller signs off holds over the firm's threshold[^10]. If every mismatch gets the same treatment, a rules workflow does it cheaper[^6][^8].

watchOuts: Buying a relabeled chatbot: Gartner calls this agent washing and counts only about 130 real agentic vendors[^6][^8]. Ask for a demo where it chooses its own steps on a case it hasn't seen.

Giving the agent more access than the task needs: coding agents at Replit and PocketOS deleted production databases[^19][^20]. Grant the narrowest permissions, and no delete or payment rights without a person[^10].

Treating an instruction as a control: Replit's code freeze was only an instruction, and NIST saw hijack success reach 81%[^19][^13]. Enforce limits in permissions and approval steps, not in the prompt[^11].
Expecting long tasks to finish unattended: the best agent fully finished 30.3% of simulated office tasks[^14][^16]. Keep each task short and add checkpoints where a person looks.

No baseline, then a surprise bill: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic projects canceled by 2027 over cost, unclear value or weak controls[^6]. Measure time and error rate first, and model per-action costs from our check[^33].

The wrong person confirms: Agentforce's confirmation asks the user in the conversation, who may be your customer[^24]. Route refunds and payment changes to a named role in an approval queue[^30][^31][^22].

faq.q: Which workflow should we give an agent first?
faq.a: A high-volume, well-defined one with clear rules and a low cost of error, such as order status[^8][^23]. Keep money and account changes with a person[^10][^25]. Pilot it on one team, with one owner and one measured number.

faq.q: Is "AI agent" just rebadged chatbot marketing?
faq.a: Sometimes. Gartner calls it agent washing and estimates only about 130 real agentic vendors among thousands[^6]. Ask the vendor to show the agent choosing its own steps on a new case[^8].

faq.q: Is agentic AI safe to use in a business?
faq.a: With limits. Give it the narrowest access and require a person to approve high-impact actions[^10][^11]. Gartner says fully autonomous agents are not ready for most enterprise uses[^7].

faq.q: What's the difference between RPA and agentic AI?
faq.a: RPA (robotic process automation) follows fixed rules; an agent decides its own steps[^5]. Gartner's advice: automation for routine workflows, agents when decisions are needed[^6][^8].

faq.q: Is ChatGPT generative AI or agentic AI?
faq.a: Both, depending on the feature. Chat is generative AI; ChatGPT Work runs tasks in a cloud browser and asks before hard-to-reverse steps[^2][^25].

faq.q: Is agentic AI the same as AI agents?
faq.a: Close. An AI agent is one system doing a task; agentic AI often means several agents working toward one goal[^3][^32]. Both usually run on a generative model that plans and calls tools[^4][^5].

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the process is standard, such as service desk, order status or IT tickets, and you have no AI engineers[^17]. MIT found bought tools and partnerships reached deployment about 67% of the time, against about 33% for internal builds (self-reported)[^17]. Many agents now ship inside software you already pay for[^21][^23].
buyVsBuild.build: Build or configure when your own data and rules are the edge, and you need control of the approval gate and the activity log[^12][^10]. Start with a fixed workflow and add agent steps only where needed[^5]. Platforms such as Copilot Studio, Agentforce and UiPath are a middle path: you configure, they host[^21][^23][^31].

pickElse: The steps never change: use rules automation, such as Power Automate or UiPath robots[^6][^8]. Agents trade cost and speed for flexibility you won't need[^5].
You need one smart step inside a fixed process: use a workflow with a single AI step to classify, extract or draft[^5]. That runs on a predefined path, not an agent's own plan[^5].
The process itself is broken: fix the form, the handoff or the data first[^8]. Gartner warns that agents bolted onto old processes cap the return[^8].
You need a score or forecast, not content or actions: that is predictive AI. See our generative AI vs predictive AI comparison.

offer.heading: Not sure if a workflow needs an agent?
offer.body: In 30 minutes we map one of your workflows step by step. We mark which steps suit an assistant, an agent or plain automation, and who approves each. You leave with a short plan and the questions to ask vendors.

reviews.notes: Gets the operator's question from the title and a three-way answer (assistant, agent, neither) in the bottom line. The workflow table names an owner per row, which is what she'd forward. Recipes 2 and 3 had no before-and-after measure; added a baseline step to each (resolution time; exception count and handling time). The research has no sourced time-to-deploy figure, so none is given.

Reads on a phone. Acronyms SOP, PO, ERP, AP, RPA, CRM and P&L appeared bare; spelled out or swapped for plain words at first use. Own-data table is five columns, so product names were shortened (vendor in brackets) and the charging cells trimmed to fit 390px. Zendesk cell said 'human agent', confusing next to AI agents; now 'a person'.

Wants to know if one team can pilot first and what it costs per unit. Added 'Pilot it on one team, with one owner and one measured number' to the first-workflow FAQ. Per-seat vs per-action pricing sits side by side in the workflow table and the own-data check, with a 15-person seat example ($315 a month) in recipe 1. No sourced margin figure exists for a firm this size, so none is claimed.

Read as controller and head of service. Controller needs payments kept with a person and a log to audit: payments row says a person does the step, recipe 3 bars payment release and the controller now reviews 'the log of agent actions' (was 'activity log'). Head of service needs billing rules: added 'handoffs free' to the Zendesk price. The wrong-person-confirms watch-out covers customer-side confirmation.

Steve gets the answer in 10 seconds: question title and five short bullets. Cost is answered with dated list prices or 'not published'; security in the safe-to-use FAQ and the access watch-outs; skills in buy-or-build. 'Consequential actions' in the key numbers read as jargon; now 'risky actions'. Bottom-line claim that rules automation is cheaper now cites the practitioner cost note. No case from a firm his size and no Zavient price for the next step exist in the research, so neither is claimed.
